f: Protein language model embeddings group residues by hydrophobicity and charge without being told the properties of amino acids, and recover which residues make physical contact in the folded structure.
ESMFold predicts atomic-level structure from a single sequence. AlphaFold, which also uses alignments of related sequences, reached near-experimental accuracy in the blind CASP14 assessment.
SaProt generalizes by pairing each amino acid with a token for its local structure.
GPN-MSA adds aligned sequences from 100 vertebrate genomes, making conservation visible, and outperforms sequence-only models at predicting deleterious variants.
UCE represents each gene by the ESM2 embedding of its protein rather than by a fixed gene list, so it can place cells from species absent from training in a shared space.
Protein language model likelihoods partly reflect how often related sequences were sampled across the tree of life rather than fitness alone.

LLM-based gene annotators may score well on benchmarks partly because curated databases shaped both their training and the benchmark labels, and they perform worse on orphan genes and non-model organisms.
AlphaFold2 relies heavily on related sequences and largely fails to predict the structural disruption caused by destabilizing point mutations.
Larger protein language models do not consistently improve zero-shot fitness prediction.
Downstream tasks often reuse features learned early in pretraining.
Protein language model likelihoods predict mutational effects without training on mutational data and correlate with deep mutational scanning measurements.
EVE, an unsupervised model of evolutionary variation, matched or exceeded supervised methods at classifying human variants as pathogenic or benign.

Autoregressive training made design possible: ProGen produced artificial lysozymes with measurable catalytic activity, and ESM3, prompted with structure and function tokens, generated a fluorescent protein distant from known natural sequences.
Enformer predicts regulatory signals across the genome well, yet it poorly explains differences in gene expression between individuals and often predicts even the wrong direction of effect.
A 2026 preprint reports the same personal-genome gap for AlphaGenome and Borzoi.
In predicting responses to genetic perturbations, simple linear models and even the average of the training data match or outperform foundation models.
Geneformer and scGPT embeddings did not outperform simple baselines without fine-tuning.
An L1-regularized logistic regression rivaled scBERT on its reported task.
Parameter-free representations match single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks.
Simple baselines rival protein language models in mutation-dense design of function tasks.
In multi-omics integration, foundation models showed no uniform advantage across 23 methods.
DNA language models are spread across competing benchmarks, on which they showed inconsistent gains over lightweight supervised models.
Common perturbation metrics are dominated by systematic expression differences unrelated to the specific perturbation, so a model can score well simply by predicting an average response.

When metrics are calibrated against both an uninformative mean baseline and a positive control, several deep-learning perturbation models do outperform simple baselines, so part of the reported parity reflects the metric rather than the model.
AlphaMissense showed meaningful discordance with curated clinical evidence across 5,845 missense variants in 59 disease genes.
Structure-confidence scores poorly separated successes from failures among 614 experimentally characterized de novo protein designs.
Most of 21 pretrained RNA language models did not outperform a one-hot encoding for secondary-structure prediction once closely related sequences were removed from the test set.

Independent evaluation concentrates on protein sequence, single-cell representation and perturbation prediction. Bulk transcriptomics has no dedicated foundation-model benchmark, spatial benchmarks are only emerging, and multi-omics and RNA models have few head-to-head comparisons.
x: Bulk, spatial, multi-omics and RNA models

f: Sparse autoencoders have recovered features for active sites, zinc-finger domains and disulfide bonds in protein language models.
Simulated gene deletion with Geneformer nominated therapeutic targets for cardiomyopathy that were then supported experimentally.
General protein language models guided antibody evolution toward improved binding without task-specific training.

Sparse-autoencoder dictionaries so far cover only a few protein and genomic models, so for most models it remains unknown whether a correct prediction reflects real biology or a shortcut that happens to work on the test.
Independent evaluations show that current agents remain brittle on realistic analysis tasks.

In BioReason, an LLM alone reached 90% on pathway questions and the encoder made little difference. On variant classification the LLM reached 49%; adding Evo 2 raised this to 80%, compared with 61% for Nucleotide Transformer.
Paper2Agent’s AlphaGenome tools outperformed general agents, showing that packaging matters.
At an LDL cholesterol locus, the AlphaGenome agent prioritized SORT1, whereas the original paper emphasized CELSR2 and PSRC1.
Agent benchmarks test general bioinformatics analysis, not whether an agent chooses the right foundation model or interprets its output correctly.
When controls that separate the encoder’s contribution from the LLM’s were applied to six systems, BioReason and BioReason-Pro were as accurate with shuffled biological inputs as with intact ones.
